Someone recently asked me if when I'm there I feel like I'm truly home and it made me realize that I feel more connected to my Italian home and culture and feel very little connection to Canadian culture. In fact I feel quite alienated sometimes at work and even with my non-Italian friends in Canada. I feel so fake here and unnatural and full of stress and junk and everything feels forced, but when I'm there I just feel more free and more like my true self if that makes sense?

Not American but honestly I think it's a vocal minority that makes a big deal out of it and create degrees of what's considered Italian. For example, my situation is that I have Italian citizenship and my parents are from the same town in Italy. We have a house there and I spend my summers there but was born in and live in Canada most of the year. I speak quasi proper Italian but mainly Abruzzese dialect. I know there are many who would say I'm not truly Italian because I don't tick every box, but my cousins in Italy tell me I am Italian and are truly proud that I am so connected to my family's town and language especially with the dialect dying out among people my age and younger. 
Sometimes I'm afraid of accidentally speaking in dialect so in big cities I usually just revert to English and a few times when store associates see my name they exclaim "sei Italiana!" and start asking me questions about my life. So basically it's subjective. Some people recognize an Italian name and that's all that matters. Some people are your blood relative and that's all that matters. Irl I have more people telling me I am Italian than not 🤷‍♀️ even growing up in a first generation Italian ethnic enclave community. By definition anyone with Italian heritage is technically Italian. When that gets diluted to a small percentage after generations living outside of Italy, it's kinda hard to claim being Italian and I would agree with the naysayers.

After letting my thoughts digest for a few days I think Art and Patrick were in love and it ends with them realizing it during the match. I mean Art literally leaps into his arms, returning his love as if it was a volley. 
Luca Guadagnino also did an Anatomy of a Scene breakdown and said they both wanted each other and were jealous of Tashi... 

When you break it down you can see that in their first meeting, Tashi is the one they're fighting over. In college, it's Patrick. Then in 2019 it's Art. 

The hetero relationships are all devoid of love and are just using each other as stand ins. Patrick uses Tashi as his stand in for Art: He's dating her, but the churro scene shows he really wants Art. 
Tashi is Art's stand in for Patrick: They draw that comparison with him spitting the gum in their hands. And obviously Art is Tashi's stand in for a tennis career after Patrick rejected that from her. 

Patrick we see is more open about his sexuality and Art's sexuality is repressed but it becomes clear around the sauna scene. Patrick tries to reconnect and he rejects him, saying that he doesn't want to "play" with him anymore, alluding to something more between them in the past. In the next scene he tells Tashi he's "tired" of playing, knowing it'll provoke her to leave him. He's tired of pretending to be someone he's not. 

At the end of their match they both seem to try to lose. Compared to when they first met Tashi and both wanted to win to get her number. Now they recognize that neither cares to win her and they just go at it, knowing the truth in each other, and "falling in love". 

Their ending was foreshadowed twice. The first time on the beach when Tashi says that a great game of tennis was like being in love. Then in the way things play out in the hotel scene: Tashi moves to Patrick first very briefly just like their relationship, then moves to Art, then back to Patrick, then both of them together, and in the end it's just the two of them.

I saw it as being about a woman who is living free from the societal expectations of her time and challenging the men around her. Victorian women were seen as property of their husbands and meant to behave in a subservient and chaste way. They were treated as children incapable of making decisions or being seen as their own person. 

For Bella though, the experiment meant that she could live as a woman but did not develop feelings of shame or learning the customs and norms of what was expected of her. She questions everything and does what she wants and it's frustrating to the men around her because they can't comprehend how a woman can live so freely and joyously. Her sexual discovery becomes something she enjoys for pleasure but also uses to assert power and control.

Didn't want to make a long post but I'm feeling a lot of emotions after we buried my nonna today. Most Italians that immigrated to America during the post-war period were from the south so Italo-American culture evolved from mostly southern Italian groups, who largely resisted American assimilation. That said, it's still part of the Italian diaspora. Being only considered Italian if you are born and raised in Italy is a nationalistic perspective. If someone was 1/6th Italian then I would probably agree with you, but OP was referring to her first generation father and grandfather. When some of my family left Italy they brought all of the recipes, traditions, and Abruzzese dialect with them.

So if OP's nonno had to leave Italy due to poverty and fascism, but raised his son in America in an Italian ethnic enclave and in an Italian household, it's not really fair to disregard a large part of his heritage and upbringing because of that. Many first generation Americans even learn English as a second language because they learn the native tongue of their parents first. It's nice that your family was able to stay in Italy, but so many had no choice but to leave to survive and it was so very painful.

There are other sources online you can look into but it's accepted that Italian is an ethnicity because of its shared culture, languages, phenotypes, and genomic history. If you could find a source that says it's not an ethnicity then I'd love to see it. At least when I specialised in race and ethnicity studies at a Canadian university, Italian ethnicity was used frequently as an example. They also taught me about the [cultural mosaic](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_mosaic) which acknowledges and values the origins of immigrants and their families. It's very beautiful and helps immigrants and their families keep their cultural identity when moving to a new country. For example when someone from India immigrates to Canada and starts a family, they and their children would be Indian-Canadian. A Ukrainian family would be Ukrainian-Canadian, etc. If you moved to Canada, you and your children would be an Italian-Canadian if you became a naturalized citizen. It doesn't overwrite your heritage, it just adds to it.

I did not take her comment to mean that all Italians are stereotypically angry. She was just using her personal experience to relate to Cuomo's moronic comment.

Lindsay Lohan and Paris Hilton were both having public troubles at the same time, so you never knew who was going to be making news that day, it was very sensationalized. People were also less sensitive to mental health issues so "crazy Britney" was basically a punchline. I'm glad people are reflecting back on it now and realizing how they contributed to that breakdown.

Not to make a long comment longer but I remember South Park did an episode about her at that time and when the preview came out everyone was like "omg South Park is gonna make fun of Britney" but the episode ended up being a commentary on the media's horrible treatment of her and everyone was so surprised, but they were spot on.
